title: Bisection and certified root brackets
terms: bisection method; sign-changing bracket; intermediate value theorem; bisection error bound.

exposition.text:
For continuous f on [a, b] with f (a)f(b) < 0, bisection tests the midpoint and retains a half-
interval with opposite endpoint signs, unless it finds an exact zero. Continuity guarantees a
root in every retained bracket. A sign change is sufficient for a root, but not necessary: an even-
multiplicity root need not change signs.
n n+1
After n halvings the bracket length is (b − a)/2 ; its midpoint is within (b − a)/2 of a root in
the bracket. State the iteration-count convention to avoid off-by-one errors. Bisection converges
reliably under its hypotheses but reduces interval width only by a fixed factor at each step.

Apply three bisection halvings to f(x) = x − 2 starting with [1, 2]. What is the midpoint of the
resulting bracket?
(A) 9/8 (B) 19/16 (C) 5/4 (D) 21/16 (E) 11/8

solution.text:
Testing 3/2 gives a positive value, leaving [1, 3/2]. Testing 5/4 gives 125/64 − 2 < 0, leaving
[5/4, 3/2]. Testing 11/8 gives a positive value, leaving [5/4, 11/8]. Its midpoint is 21/16.

rule is applied repeatedly. What happens?

(B) The method reaches a zero after finitely many steps.
(C) The bracket lengths fail to tend to zero.
(D) The method must converge to one.
√

solution.text:

Every retained interval has its negative endpoint below 2 and its positive endpoint at or
√
above it. Its width halves, so the endpoints and midpoints converge to 2. But f takes
only the values minus one and one. The missing continuity hypothesis, rather than any
error in halving the interval, invalidates the root guarantee.

question.text:
Apply bisection to f(x) = (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3) starting with [0, 5]. To which root do the retained
brackets converge?
(A) 1
(B) 2
(C) 3
(D) The method must alternate among all three roots.
(E) The limit depends on a free choice at every step.

solution.text:
The initial endpoint signs are negative and positive. At the first midpoint 5/2, the product
is negative, so the retained bracket is [5/2, 5]. Its only root is three. Every later retained
sign-changing bracket contains that root, and shrinking widths force convergence to it. An
initial bracket containing several roots does not make bisection find the smallest one or all
of them.

question.text:
Which hypothesis guarantees that bisection can maintain a root-containing bracket for a func-
tion on [a, b]?
(A) Differentiability on (a, b) alone
(B) Opposite endpoint signs without continuity
(C) Continuity on [a, b] and f (a)f(b) < 0
(D) Equal endpoint values
(E) Monotonicity alone

solution.text:
Continuity and opposite endpoint signs give a root by the intermediate value theorem. At
each nonzero midpoint, one half retains opposite endpoint signs and hence a root. Without
continuity, a jump can change sign without any zero.

question.text:
A continuous nonnegative function on [0, 1] has value one at each of finitely many distinct sam-
ple points x , . . . , x . What can those data establish about zeros between sample points?
1 N
(A) The function has no zero.
(B) Every zero must be at a sampled point.
(C) The function must have a sign-changing bracket.
(D) An unsampled zero is still possible, despite every sampled value being positive.
(E) There must be exactly one zero.

solution.text:
Q
Choose an unsampled point c in the interval and set P(x) = (x − x ). The polynomial
j j
2
[1 − P (x)/P (c)] is nonnegative, equals one at every sample point, and vanishes at c. In
contrast, the constant function one has identical sampled values and no zero. A zero can be
touched without a sign change, so the bisection criterion is sufficient, not necessary.
